query: Many physical and chemical fabrication approaches have produced multi-element, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles, yet their synthesis–structure–property relationships remain poorly established. This limits evaluation of their suitability for catalytic operation at 773–1173 K and thermoelectric use at 473–1923 K, including catalytic settings where low noble-metal content is desirable. What governs whether these nanoparticles preserve structural and chemical stability under such service regimes, and why? Formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis, specify a controlled intervention that separates it from competing explanations, predict observations relative to a baseline, define its boundary conditions, connect it to the prior evidence summarized above, and provide a clear falsification test.

generation.hypothesis: In multi‐element near‐equiatomic solid‐solution nanoparticles, increasing the noble‐metal content enhances structural and chemical stability under high-temperature catalytic and thermoelectric conditions by suppressing thermally induced interdiffusion and elemental segregation.
generation.material_initial_state: Near‐equiatomic multi‐element solid‐solution nanoparticles synthesized under identical conditions except for varied noble‐metal fractions.
generation.intervention: Systematically vary the noble‐metal content during nanoparticle synthesis while keeping all other synthesis parameters and overall composition ratios constant.
generation.conditions: Service conditions relevant to catalytic operation (773–1173 K) and thermoelectric use (473–1923 K).
generation.structural_mediator: The degree of elemental distribution homogeneity and defect structures, which are modulated by noble‐metal content.
generation.mechanism: Higher noble‐metal content may reduce atomic diffusivity and provide stronger interatomic bonding, thereby lessening the driving force and kinetics for high-temperature interdiffusion and phase segregation. This suppression of segregation leads to prolonged single‐phase stability and resistance to coarsening or precipitation processes.
generation.predicted_outcome: Nanoparticles with higher noble‐metal content will exhibit a more uniform elemental distribution, reduced phase segregation and coarsening, and hence superior structural and chemical stability compared to low noble‐metal content nanoparticles under the specified high-temperature conditions.
generation.baseline: Nanoparticles with low noble‐metal content, which are expected to show increased susceptibility to high-temperature-induced elemental segregation and phase instability.
generation.boundary: This effect is expected to hold for near‐equiatomic, multi‐element compositions synthesized under similar processing conditions; however, if synthesis defects or other factors predominate, the impact of noble-metal content may be diminished.
generation.uncertainty: While the general stabilizing trend with increased noble-metal content is predicted based on analogous alloy studies, the precise quantitative effects and thresholds remain uncertain and may also depend on additional synthesis and processing variables.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two sets of otherwise identical multi‐element nanoparticles that differ only in their noble‐metal content (e.g., one set with low noble-metal content and one with a higher noble-metal fraction). Subject both sets to in situ high-temperature testing (e.g., using high-temperature TEM or XRD) under conditions simulating catalytic (773–1173 K) and thermoelectric (473–1923 K) service. Compare the evolution of phase composition, elemental segregation, and morphology over time.
measurements: Elemental mapping (e.g., EDS) to assess homogeneity
XRD analysis to monitor phase changes or precipitation
TEM imaging for morphological changes and coarsening evaluation
Performance metrics relevant to catalytic or thermoelectric function
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If nanoparticles with higher noble-metal content do not demonstrate statistically significant improvements in maintaining single-phase homogeneity and resisting phase segregation or coarsening compared to the low noble-metal baseline under these temperatures, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Materials performance is central to the satisfactory operation of current and future nuclear energy systems due to the severe irradiation environment in reactors. Searching for structural materials with excellent irradiation tolerance is crucial for developing the next generation nuclear reactors. Here, we report the irradiation responses of a novel multi-component alloy system, high entropy alloy (HEA) Al x CoCrFeNi ( x = 0.1, 0.75 and 1.5), focusing on their precipitation behavior. It is found that the single phase system, Al 0.1 CoCrFeNi, exhibits a great phase stability against ion irradiation. No precipitate is observed even at the highest fluence. In contrast, numerous coherent precipitates are present in both multi-phase HEAs. Based on the irradiation-induced/enhanced precipitation theory, the excellent structural stability against precipitation of Al 0.1 CoCrFeNi is attributed to the high configurational entropy and low atomic diffusion, which reduces the thermodynamic driving force and kinetically restrains the formation of precipitate, respectively. Unlike other conventional alloys based on a “principal element,” high-entropy alloy (HEA) is a unique material that maintains a random solid solution structure without forming intermetallic compounds in operating temperatures due to its high configurational entropy [1] – [3] . It also has outstanding physical and chemical properties, which makes it a potential replacement for traditional metallic materials, and it has recently been referred to as a multi-principal element alloy (MPEA) or compositionally concentrated alloy (CCA) [4] – [9] .

As attention in HEAs increases, many studies have been conducted to explore its mechanical, physical and chemical properties [10] – [15] . In particular, equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi HEA, which was the first developed HEA, is the most studied because of its excellent combination of tensile strength and elongation along with excellent fracture toughness and corrosion resistance [6] , [16] – [21] . However, despite the advantages of equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi HEA, many issues arise owing to its low yield strength and costly and complex thermomechanical processing (i.e., multiple casting → hot rolling → homogenization → cold rolling → annealing → cutting, etc.

decision.trend: Early studies in high‐entropy alloy systems have mapped how synthesis and processing influence phase stability. For example, PMC4999872 showed that near‐equiatomic, single‐phase alloys resist precipitation under irradiation, whereas multiphase compositions readily form coherent precipitates that grow with treatment. Later, PMC10213035 demonstrated that step‐wise thermo‐mechanical processing can tailor coherent precipitate structures in refractory HEAs, indicating that fine control over elemental distribution and defect structures can modulate stability and mechanical response. However, these studies—though advanced in bulk or film geometries—leave open how synthesis–structure–property relations play out in metastable, multi‐element, nanostructured solid solutions, particularly under high‐temperature catalytic and thermoelectric regimes and when noble-metal content is kept low.
decision.unsolved: It remains unsolved whether the observed stability (or lack thereof) in these nanoparticle systems is primarily governed by intrinsic limitations in homogenizing the elemental distribution during synthesis, or by high‐temperature‐driven interdiffusion and segregation (potentially exacerbated by low noble‐metal content) that leads to phase separation or coarsening. In other words, the mechanistic link between synthesis parameters (e.g., distribution of noble metals) and long‐term structural and chemical stability under service conditions has yet to be decisively established.
decision.why: Based on the trend where controlled synthesis and processing have been used to govern phase stability (as seen in single‐phase versus multiphase responses in bulk or film studies), the most plausible next step is to design a controlled experiment that systematically varies the noble-metal content in these near‐equiatomic nanoparticles. By synthesizing otherwise identical nanoparticles that differ only in their noble-metal fractions, and by subjecting them to in situ high-temperature structural characterization (e.g., high-temperature TEM or XRD during catalytic/thermoelectric operation), the intervention directly tests whether the lower noble-metal content triggers accelerated elemental segregation or phase evolution under service conditions. This approach occupies the performance limitation niche and follows the literature’s move toward using controlled composition synthesis to isolate key mechanisms, providing a clear falsification test if no significant stability differences are observed relative to a noble-metal–rich baseline.
